title: Imo the sweet-potato-washing macaque
hook: A young monkey started washing her food, and her whole troop picked up the habit.
peek: In 1953 a young macaque named Imo, on a small Japanese island, began rinsing sand off sweet potatoes. Her family copied her, then her playmates, until within a few years most of the young monkeys were doing it.
lede: On Koshima, a small island in southern Japan, researchers began leaving sweet potatoes on the beach for a troop of wild macaques in the early 1950s. In 1953 a young female about a year and a half old, whom they called Imo, started dipping her sandy potatoes in water and rubbing them clean. Nobody taught her. Soon others began to copy.

bullets.text: Imo's mother and playmates picked it up first. Within a few years most of the young monkeys were washing their potatoes. Adult males, who spent less time with the youngsters, were the slowest to join in.

Imo first washed her potatoes in a freshwater stream. Over time the troop moved to washing them in the sea, and many monkeys took to dipping each bite in salt water between mouthfuls, which may be for the taste.

A few years later Imo made a second discovery. Wheat thrown on the beach was mixed with sand, so she scooped up handfuls and dropped them in the water. The sand sank, the grains floated, and she picked them off the surface.

A popular 1970s story claimed that once enough monkeys learned the trick, it leapt by itself to other islands. That part is folklore. The real records show a slow, ordinary spread, one monkey watching another.
